title: a commit is a checkpoint, shipping is live verification
description: A field note on why clean commits do not equal shipped software, and why live customer-visible verification defines completion.
tldr: a commit is a checkpoint. shipping means verifying that the product, route, or behavior works live where customers can see it.

body: shipped means the work has been verified live. The repository can be clean while the product, route, or behavior remains broken.
The useful finish line is customer-visible evidence that the change works in the real product.

sections.h2: why can a clean repo still hide broken work?
body: A clean repository records a checkpoint in the code. It does not prove that the running product reflects that checkpoint or that the intended behavior works.
That gap is where teams can mistake completed development work for a finished product change.

sections.h2: what should a team verify before calling something finished?
body: Verify the live product, the relevant route, or the behavior customers are meant to use. The question is whether customers can see it working.
If customers cannot see the result working, the work remains unfinished regardless of the repository state.

sections.h2: how should we define shipping for our team?
body: Define shipped around live verification and customer visibility. A commit can mark progress, while live evidence marks completion.
The definition should make clear what working means in the product customers actually encounter.

faqs.q: does a clean git commit mean the feature is shipped?
faqs.a: A clean commit marks a checkpoint in the repository. Shipping requires live verification that the product, route, or behavior works.

faqs.q: what is the difference between committing and shipping software?
faqs.a: Committing records code progress. Shipping confirms that customers can see the intended result working live.

faqs.q: how do you know when software work is finished?
faqs.a: The work is finished when the relevant product, route, or behavior has been verified live and customers can see it working.

faqs.q: what should shipped mean for a software team?
faqs.a: Shipped should mean live, customer-visible verification. Each team should define the evidence that proves the intended result works.
